About Me

"Real learning isn’t what people remember after the training; it’s what they do differently, and keep doing."

I’m a human-centered instructional designer who begins every project by asking what is really getting in the way of performance, and brings in AI only where that analysis shows it belongs. Over fifteen years of teaching and instructional design, across more than ten industries, I have learned that training succeeds only when people do something differently afterward. My path began in 2008 in front of engineering students in India and moved through ESL, higher education, and eLearning for global clients.

That first classroom left me with a question I couldn’t shake: why does so little of what is taught actually stay? It is still my starting point. My 4Ps answer it: Process to understand the problem, Practice to apply the learning, Perform to demonstrate the results, and Persist to make the change last.

Research

Research Area

An AI-Ready Needs Analysis (ARNA) for Learning Design

In Progress

What Do Designers Need to Ask in Front-End Analysis When AI Is Part of the Work?

Advisor: Dr. Mike Law. I am conducting this study under his guidance.

A qualitative study of what experienced instructional designers ask, omit, or wish they had asked during front-end analysis for AI-enhanced projects. The planned result is a short practitioner protocol that extends classic front-end analysis (Rossett; Mager & Pipe) with questions about which gaps people should close through learning and which an AI tool should handle.

  • RQ1What questions do instructional design practitioners ask, omit, or wish they had asked during front-end analysis in AI-enhanced contexts?
  • RQ2What does an ARNA protocol look like when it is built from practitioner input and refined by member checking?
  • StatusIRB application in preparation. The research protocol, consent form and interview guide are drafted. Interviews have not started.
Funding
Submitted

AI Tools in IELTS Test Preparation and Washback Effects: Investigating Learner Behaviour, Self-Regulation, and Construct Validity

Funder and Program

IELTS Joint-Funded Research Programme, Test Impact / Washback category.

Research Team

Dr. Ramya Devi Bommanaboina (NIT Warangal, India), Dr. Lalitha Devi Bommanaboina (SR University, India) and Vimala Telu (Georgia State University, USA).

Core Question

How are IELTS candidates and teachers in India and the United States using generative AI tools in test preparation without formal guidance, and what washback effects does this have on learning behaviour, self-regulation and the construct validity of IELTS?

About the Study

An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study across two contrasting contexts: a coaching-centre-driven preparation market in India and university ESL and community programmes in the United States. A survey of candidates and teachers maps AI-use patterns and self-regulation, and interviews explain them. The framework draws on washback theory, self-regulated learning and sociocultural theory.

My Role

US-based researcher: instrument design, quantitative and qualitative data analysis, integration of findings and report writing.

Status

Proposal submitted. Awaiting decision.

Toward Sociocultural AI for Education: A Case Study from a Graduate Course on Redesigning AI for Education

Conference

International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) Annual Meeting.

Core Question

What could sociocultural AI tools for education look like when educators critique and redesign them, and how does that experience change the way we think about AI in education?

About the Paper

A collaborative autoethnography by students and their instructor from a graduate Learning Sciences course in which students critiqued and redesigned educational AI tools through a sociocultural lens. The paper identifies themes across eight redesign projects and reflects on how the course shaped our thinking about AI in education. It offers concrete illustrations of what sociocultural AI tools could look like from educators’ perspectives, and guidance for teaching and learning with AI.

Authors

Eight student co-authors from the Sociocultural and Design-Based Foundations course, with Dr. Ben Shapiro, course instructor.

Status

Submitted. Awaiting decision.

Awards
2nd Place · Oral Presentation

2026 Graduate Conference for Research, Scholarship & Creative Activity

Presentation Title

AI-Powered Personalization in Maker Education for K–12 Assessment

Core Question

How can AI ethically support the assessment of creativity, collaboration and iterative learning processes in K–12 maker education?

Framework Presented

The AI-Supported Maker Learning & Assessment Framework (AIM-LAF), a conceptual model that makes hidden learning processes visible to teachers.

Key Ideas
  • Four pillars: personalized learning pathways, creativity support, collaboration analytics and authentic assessment evidence.
  • Theory: constructionism, sociocultural theory and creativity frameworks.
  • Ethical guardrails: privacy by design, teacher-in-the-loop decisions, transparency and data minimization.
Limitations
  • The model is conceptual and has not yet been piloted.
  • Teachers need training to use it well.
Future Work
  • Design-based research cycles.
  • Prototype development.
  • Classroom pilots.

Invited Lectures
Invited Lecture · 24 April 2026 · Virtual

Consumer Psychology During Course Creation

Conference

International Conference on Integrative Horizons in Mental Health

Organization

Psych Lab, Shakti Sansthan, Haridwar, India (affiliated to the Ministry of Ayush)

Core Question

If nine in ten online learners do not finish what they start, is that a learner failure or a design failure?

What I Discussed

A 20-minute talk, The Silent Crisis in Digital Learning, on why course design is a mental health issue. I covered how learners act as consumers of experience (perception, motivation, value judgment), seven design choices linked to learner stress and burnout, what neuroscience says about safety, emotion and rest, and the shift from content delivery to whole-learner experience design. I also discussed where AI helps or harms, five practical design shifts, and a redesign case in which 9-minute modules and growth-oriented feedback addressed high dropout.

Audience

Mental health professionals, psychologists, researchers and academics attending the international conference, who bring expertise on wellbeing and learner experience that instructional design can build on.

Invited Lecture · 22 September 2026 · Online

AI Tools for LSRW: A Teacher-Led 3D Framework for Learning Design

Conference

5-Day National Faculty Development Programme on “AI in English Language Acquisition”

Organization

Faculty of English, Freshman Engineering Department, PVPSIT, Vijayawada, in collaboration with NIT Warangal

Core Question

How can teachers use AI tools for listening, speaking, reading and writing without letting the tool lead the learning?

What I Discussed

An interactive session built around my Design, Deploy, Document framework.
Design: name the LSRW skill, course outcome and expected evidence before opening any tool.
Deploy: match one AI tool to each skill (NaturalReader, Snorkl, Newsela, Grammarly, plus Otter.ai, ELSA Speak, Diffit and NotebookLM as alternatives) and check the output with the CATS rubric (Correctness, Accuracy, Tone, Specificity).
Document: capture before-and-after artifacts and the student’s accept, reject or edit note.
I also covered common pitfalls such as tool-hopping and over-trusting AI output, and used live Mentimeter polls throughout.

Audience

Faculty and educators of English and communication across engineering colleges, who teach LSRW in mixed-proficiency classrooms.
